Show Your Work: Understanding Time and Effort Reporting

Hello Morgan State University Faculty & Staff, In this module, we will review key processes for time and effort on sponsored projects at Morgan State University. Topics include what is effort reporting, why effort reporting is so important, how we source our effort data, the effort certification process, and potential errors and how to correct them. We strive to continuously review these lessons to provide up-to-date guidance on Morgan’s sponsored project processes. For questions related to the activities covered in this module that are not addressed in the module content, please contact the ORA Training and Communications Coordinator: Mr. Ryan Mobley, CRA, CFRA, CPRA Email: ryan.mobley@morgan.edu Phone: 443-885-4771 Thank you, ORA Training Team

Self-paced ORA eTraining module. Source: https://share.articulate.com/s01WpXKAGFN1dft3QDlow

## Time and Effort Defined
What is Effort Reporting?
What is Time and Effort Reporting?
Time and Effort Reporting is the formal process by which an institution verifies that the salary and wages charged to sponsored projects reasonably reflects the proportion of an individual's total institutional work devoted to those projects. It is not a record of hours worked, but a certification of effort as a percentage of total activities including research, teaching, and administrative duties.
Auditor Assurance
Effort reporting provides sufficient assurance to state and federal auditors that appropriate internal control measures actively track allocability for each sponsored project. Auditors are looking for: (1) documentation support (2) reasonableness (3) timeliness and (4) internal controls.
Federally Mandated
Effort reporting is a federally mandated requirement outlined in Code of Federal Regulations (CFR). Under which, we in the research administration reference Uniform Guidance (2CFR200) as our playbook for research compliance. 2CFR200.430 specifically details personnel compensation and effort on sponsored projects.

Effort commitments for project personnel outlined in the approved Notice of Award must be met. Significant deviation from stated effort (typically more than 25%) will required sponsor/agency review and approval.
Effort Committed but Not Met
Effort certification is federally required to be completed on at least an annual basis. Increased frequency is allowed at the institution's discretion. All effort certification requests should be verified and completed within a timely manner.

## Who Certifies Effort?
Certification: What Does it Represent?
Effort certification confirms that salary charged to a sponsored project reasonably reflects the work performed. Because this is a formal attestation, effort must be certified by someone with direct knowledge of how that work was carried out. By certifying effort, the individual is confirming that: The reported effort is a reasonable estimate of work performed Salary charged to the project is appropriate and aligned with institutional policy All institutional activities are reflected within 100% total effort
Complete the content above before moving on.
Types of Certifiers
Primary Certifier
Primary Certifier: The individual The preferred and most direct method is for faculty and staff to certify their own effort whenever possible. The individual employee is best positioned to confirm: How their time was actually spent How effort was distributed across activities Faculty do not need to certify salary received from (1) their academic term contract or (2) summer session teaching contracts.
Alternate Certifier
Alternate Certifier: Knowledgeable Designee A designee may be assigned to certify project effort for employees only if they have first-hand knowledge of the individual's work. Typical Designees: (1) Project PI (2) Dean or Department Chair (3) Program Manager.

## Significance of Effort Reporting
Effort Certification: Institutional Impact
Effort reporting is more than an administrative requirement. It is a formal certification that salary charged to a sponsored project reasonably reflects the work performed. When effort is not certified accurately or in a timely manner, the consequences can extend beyond one project and place the university's federal funding, audit standing, reputation, and future grant eligibility at risk.
Complete the content above before moving on.
Key Institutional Risks
Disallowed Costs and Repayment
If salary charges cannot be supported by accurate effort certification, the sponsor may determine that the costs are unallowable. The university may be required to repay those costs, including associated fringe benefits and indirect costs.
Increased Federal Scrutiny
Poor effort reporting can lead to additional sponsor review, expanded audits, corrective action plans, and stricter award conditions. Under 2CFR200.339 , federal agencies may withhold payments, disallow costs, suspend or terminate awards, initiate suspension/debarment proceedings, withhold future federal funds, or pursue other legal remedies.
Loss of Current or Future Funding
Federal agencies may suspend or terminate awards and may withhold new or continuation funding when noncompliance is serious or unresolved.
Suspension or Debarment Risk
In serious cases, federal agencies may initiate suspension or debarment proceedings. This can affect an institution's ability to receive federal grants, contracts, or other federal funding.
The False Claims Act
The False Claims Act, sometimes called The Lincoln Law, is a federal civil fraud law used to recover funds when an entity knowingly submits, or causes the submission of, false or fraudulent claims for payment to the federal government. This can include knowingly charging salary to an award when certified effort does not support the charge. The False Claims Act can result in significant financial penalties, including damages and penalties per false claim. The Justice Department recovered over $6.8 billion in False Claims Act cases in 2019.

## Institutional Base Salary (IBS)
What is Institutional Base Salary (IBS)?
Institutional Base Salary (IBS) is the total annual compensation paid by the institution for an individual's appointment, whether that time is spent on research, teaching, administrative duties, or other institutional activities.
IBS represents 100% of an individual's institutional effort.
It is the basis for calculating salary charges to sponsored projects.
It is not based on hours worked, but on total institutional responsibilities.

Institutional Base Salary: Contract Restrictions
Faculty Contracts & IBS
For 9.5-month faculty, IBS consists of: (1) their 9.5-month academic year salary , and (2) up to 2.5 months of summer salary . This means faculty may receive additional compensation on sponsored projects during the summer months, but only within defined limits. Key Restrictions Total effort across all activities cannot exceed 100% IBS. Summer salary is limited to 26.3% of the faculty's academic-year salary. Faculty cannot "stack" multiple summer appointments beyond the 2.5-month limit.
Staff Contracts & IBS
For 12-month faculty and staff, IBS is defined as their full 12-month institutional salary , which already represents 100% effort . Key Restrictions Individuals cannot exceed 100% IBS Secondary contracts for additional pay on sponsored projects are not allowable Instead of additional compensation, release time or effort reallocation is possible. Administrative/clerical salaries cannot be charged directly when: (1) the work is routine (e.g., general admin support), (2) the role supports multiple projects or departments broadly, or (3) it is not specifically justified and approved in writing. Key Exceptions: Uniform Guidance Under 2CFR200.413(c) , the university is reimbursed for the cost of administrative and clerical salaries through the recovery of indirect costs on sponsored awards. However, they may be charged directly to a federal award only if specific conditions are met. The work must be essential to carrying out the project's programmatic objectives. For example, managing a complex training program with many participants. The role must be explicitly included in the proposal budget and justified to the sponsor. The sponsor must approve the cost either at the time of award or through prior written approval. The same cost cannot be charged both directly and through indirect cost recovery.

  - Pay through employee via a stipend request  [incorrect]
  - Reallocate an equal portion of the employee's regular effort to the NSF award  [CORRECT ANSWER]
  - Charge the employee's time without adjusting their regular workload  [incorrect]
  If correct: Great job!
